title: Strategy Versus Execution
description: Translating changing business strategy into engineering priorities, **operating mechanisms**, and explicit stop-doing decisions.

competency.name: Strategy Versus Execution
competency.definition: Connects technology plans to business strategy and adjusts execution when the business context changes.
competency.whyItMatters: Senior leaders must do more than describe strategy; they must convert it into priorities, mechanisms, and **trade-offs**.

prompt.primary: Tell me about a time you translated business strategy into a technology roadmap.
variants: Give me an example of when you changed engineering priorities because the business context changed.
Tell me about a time you stopped important engineering work because it no longer matched company strategy.
interviewerIntent: Does the candidate understand commercial context?
Can they stop or defer work, not just add work?
Do they connect roadmap changes to measurable business outcomes?

scenario.signatureExample: A CTO at a B2B SaaS company realizes enterprise deals are blocked by security, integration, and deployment gaps.
context: Several platform projects are technically interesting but not unlocking revenue.
Sales is losing enterprise deals because of auditability and identity gaps.
Engineering teams distrust roadmap shifts that look like sales interruptions.
constraints: Enterprise revenue is a company-level priority.
Teams need a credible reason to pause internal platform work.
Security and integration work must become productized capability, not custom work.

storyAnatomy.situation: The company strategy shifted toward enterprise expansion, but the engineering roadmap still reflected earlier self-serve priorities.
storyAnatomy.task: Reframe engineering priorities so the roadmap supported enterprise revenue without becoming a custom-feature queue.
action: Mapped lost and delayed deals to missing platform capabilities.
Paused lower-leverage internal projects and explained the opportunity cost.
Created a roadmap around auditability, identity integration, deployment controls, and customer administration.
Defined **decision rules** for future enterprise commitments.
result: Enterprise blockers became a product roadmap rather than scattered escalations.
Sales and product had clearer rules for what engineering would support.
The company improved enterprise readiness while preserving platform coherence.
storyAnatomy.reflection: The hard part was not choosing enterprise work; it was making the stop-doing decisions explicit enough that teams trusted the change.
systemChange: Roadmap review tied to business segment strategy.
Quarterly measurement of revenue blockers and platform capabilities.

exampleStories.title: Enterprise Readiness Roadmap
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time you translated business strategy into a technology roadmap.
exampleStories.situation: A SaaS company shifted from self-serve growth to enterprise expansion, but enterprise deals were blocked by auditability, identity integration, and deployment controls.
strongAnswerSketch: Map lost deals and delayed opportunities to missing platform capabilities.
Pause lower-leverage internal platform work and explain the opportunity cost.
Define a roadmap around reusable enterprise capabilities rather than custom features.
Create intake rules for future enterprise commitments.
whyItWorks: Connects engineering priorities to business strategy.
Shows the courage to stop work, not only add work.
Protects platform coherence while responding to revenue pressure.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I asked teams to support enterprise requests faster and added security work to the roadmap.
followUpAngles: How did you prevent custom work from taking over?

exampleStories.title: Growth To Profitability Pivot
exampleStories.promptVariant: Give me an example of when you changed engineering priorities because the business context changed.
exampleStories.situation: The company moved from growth at all costs to profitability, and engineering had to reduce infrastructure cost while preserving customer-facing roadmap commitments.
strongAnswerSketch: Translate the financial target into service-level cost ownership and product **trade-offs**.
Rank cost opportunities by customer risk, engineering effort, and recurring savings.
Pair platform efficiency work with product milestones instead of running an isolated cost program.
Introduce monthly cost reviews owned by service teams.
whyItWorks: Shows commercial understanding beyond feature delivery.
Makes cost reduction an **operating model** change.
Balances short-term financial needs with customer reliability.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I told teams to reduce cloud spend by 20 percent and asked platform engineering to find savings.
followUpAngles: What customer risk did you refuse to take?
How did teams own their costs?

strongAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate shows business understanding, prioritization discipline, and the ability to turn strategy into operating decisions.
moves: Explains the business shift and why the old roadmap no longer fit.
Names what was stopped, delayed, or reduced.
Connects engineering work to revenue, risk, customer trust, or market position.
Protects product/platform coherence while responding to commercial pressure.

weakAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate talks strategy abstractly but cannot show how it changed execution, **trade-offs**, or operating cadence.
redFlags: No clear business outcome is tied to the roadmap.
Everything becomes a priority, so no **trade-off** is visible.
Sales, product, or finance are described as distractions rather than stakeholders.
The answer presents a one-time reprioritization with no governance change.

followUps.question: What work did you stop or defer, and how did you explain it?
Which business metrics told you the roadmap needed to change?
Who resisted the change, and what did you do?
What changed in your **planning process** afterward?

signals.name: Commercial Judgment
signals.strong: Connects technology choices to business strategy and customer segments.
signals.weak: Treats the roadmap as an internal engineering artifact.

signals.name: Prioritization
signals.strong: Makes explicit stop-doing decisions with rationale.
signals.weak: Adds strategic work without removing anything.

signals.name: Operating Governance
signals.strong: Changes planning, intake, or review mechanisms so strategy keeps shaping execution.
signals.weak: Relies on a one-time roadmap reset.

rubric.expected: Connects team priorities to business goals and escalates **trade-offs** clearly.
Rebalances priorities across multiple teams and aligns product or go-to-market partners.
Converts company strategy into portfolio choices, operating cadence, and executive **trade-offs**.
Shapes technology strategy around company positioning, risk, capital allocation, and long-term leverage.

prompts.label: What changed in the business context?
What roadmap or operating decision were you accountable for?
What did you stop, start, or reframe?
Which business or execution outcomes changed?
What did you learn about strategy-to-execution translation?
What planning or governance mechanism changed?

relatedScenarios: A consumer product pivots to enterprise customers.
A cost-reduction strategy requires platform and architecture **trade-offs**.
A company shifts from growth at all costs to durable profitability.
